protocol.recent_vintage_caveat: 2025-2026 model-memory recall is expected to be incomplete/stale and is explicitly not current-state authority.
protocol.seal_rule: Search-derived facts may verify/refine/contradict these leads only in new post-seal artifacts; never rewrite the blind atlas.

cross_cycle_memory_leads.lead: Shipping repeatedly exhibits long vessel-ordering/build lags: high current earnings invite orders that arrive after demand or congestion conditions have changed, creating oversupply risk.

Nominal deadweight/TEU is not equal to effective capacity; congestion, speed, routing distance, port productivity, lay-up, blank sailings and regulation can absorb/release capacity without changing fleet size.
Cargo volume alone is insufficient: route distance and sourcing shifts can move vessel demand sharply through tonne-miles, especially for tankers, gas and bulk shipping.
Freight-rate changes often produce outsized cash-flow and asset-price moves because vessel supply is inelastic in the short run and capital costs are large.
Cheap credit/high asset values recur near order booms; downturns force deleveraging, restructurings, bank exits and transfer of vessels to stronger or new capital providers.
Commercial shipbuilding leadership shifted over decades from Europe toward Japan, then South Korea and China, with policy, scale, learning curves and financing repeatedly interacting.

Container liner economics moved toward larger ships, denser networks, alliances/VSA structures, terminal integration and consolidation, but firm-level scale savings can create industry-level overcapacity.
Ports and inland links can become the binding shipping constraint; queue/dwell/productivity changes may matter as much as fleet supply during disruptions.

Safety/environment/carbon rules can change effective supply through phase-outs, retrofits, speed changes, fuel choices and scrapping, so regulation is part of fleet economics rather than an external footnote.
Fuel prices and emissions rules repeatedly alter optimal vessel speed; slow steaming can simultaneously reduce fuel use and absorb nominal fleet capacity.
Suez, Panama, Hormuz/Persian Gulf and other chokepoints repeatedly convert geopolitics/weather into voyage-distance, insurance and effective-capacity shocks.
Containerization was a system change, not just a ship technology: it reorganized ports, inland transport, labor, inventory, carrier networks and global sourcing.
LNG and some specialized shipping historically depended more on project-linked long-term contracts than spot markets; market structure changed as commodity trading became more flexible.
A recurring high-value research target is not simply the final cycle outcome but how management, owners, shippers, lenders and investors repeatedly revised expected normalization/recovery dates.
Across cycles, participants debate whether exceptional freight earnings reflect temporary bottlenecks or durable industry structure; this Judgment/Outcome separation is a core Shipping replay target.
Scrapping, lay-up, conversions, slow steaming and deferrals are supply-side adjustment margins whose timing depends on scrap prices, vessel age, regulation, debt and expected recovery.
Orderbook-to-fleet is a necessary but insufficient forward-supply metric; delivery timing, ship size, fuel type, cancellations, yard capacity and offsetting retirements matter.
Shipping rate indices are not interchangeable: tanker Worldscale/TCE, Baltic dry indices, container spot indices and contract benchmarks differ in routes, units and market basis.

Carrier/charterer/yard/bank solvency becomes operationally important in severe downturns; Hanjin-like or restructuring episodes can affect cargo, charter coverage and asset ownership beyond freight rates.
Shipping data often arrives with publication lags or revised methodology; point-in-time replay must distinguish event/voyage time from when a participant could actually know the data.

priority_historical_judgment_families: pre-2008 freight/asset bubble versus scarcity debate
mega-ship/alliance cost logic versus oversupply risk
future_evidence_source_families: carrier/owner annual reports and historical earnings-call transcripts
port authority and canal authority historical releases
IMO convention/rule documents and implementation circulars
UNCTAD Review of Maritime Transport vintages
archived trade press only as locator/citation chase unless claim-scoped authority is adequate
historical broker/fleet/orderbook sources with exact vintage preserved

saturation.reason: Every period from the 1970s through 2026 has blind recall across the major Shipping subsectors and structural axes, plus cross-cycle patterns, Judgment targets, metrics and explicit negative space. Additional value now comes from a new model vintage or post-seal Evidence work, not unconstrained repetition within this same blind pass.
saturation.new_model_rule: A materially different model/research-instrument vintage should create a new immutable atlas and diff it as known/refined/novel rather than overwrite this one.
